title: An-Naba': the great news
hookLine: what are they asking about, the great news (78:1–2)

lines: THE FIRST SURAH OF THE JUZ'.
cards: A town where everyone is talking about the same thing, at the market, at the well, in the evenings. Some laugh. Some are angry.
Some are quietly unsettled and won't admit it. Commentators set this surah in Mecca, in a scene like that.
A man in their own town was saying that after death every person would be raised to stand and give an account, and people argued about it the way a whole city argues about one piece of news.
The surah steps into the noise and asks a question of its own. It's the first surah of the juz' this path has been reading backward, and its first word gives the whole juz' its name.

teach.b: It begins: 'amma yatasa'alun. About what are they asking one another? 'Amma is two little words run together, 'an ma, about what, and it names the whole thirtieth part of the Qur'an: Juz' 'Amma.

Then the surah answers itself: about the great news, an-naba' al-'azim, the one they disagree about. Pickthall calls it the awful tidings, awful in the old sense, full of awe. Arabic has an everyday word for news, khabar.

Al-Raghib al-Isfahani, a classical scholar of Qur'anic words, describes naba' as news of great weight, news that brings real knowledge and changes something. You don't use naba' for the weather. So what is the great news?
Ibn Kathir and others say the Resurrection, the raising of the dead and the Day of account, which the surah's first hearers disputed.
Some early commentators said the Qur'an itself, or the preaching of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

teach.h: THE RESURRECTION, THE BOOK, THE MESSENGER.
teach.b: All three hang together: a book, brought by a messenger, announcing a Day.
Then a line comes twice, and the repetition is the point: no, they will come to know; then no, they will come to know.
The surah doesn't mock the question. It takes it seriously, and instead of arguing, it turns toward the world and starts pointing.
For today, notice: the Qur'an's last part opens not with a command, but with a question people were already asking.

how: Surah an-Naba' opens the thirtieth part of the Qur'an; it is often learned by heart early and recited in the prayers, and the whole juz' is named after its first word, 'amma.

o: the river, water running to the sea
the news, news of great weight
the warning, a threat of punishment

games.q: what's inside the opening — tap the pairs.
p: the part named for the first word

s: the thirtieth part of the Qur'an is named after An-Naba's first word
all commentators agree the great news is the Qur'an
Ibn Kathir and others say the Resurrection; some said the Qur'an or the Prophet's message.
the surah mocks the people asking the question
it takes the question seriously and answers by pointing at the world.

games.q: the whole town of Mecca is arguing about the great news. what do commentators such as Ibn Kathir say it is?
o: the Resurrection and the Day of account
games.why: Ibn Kathir and others say the Resurrection; some early ones said the Qur'an or the Prophet's message. the surah answers: they will come to know.

practice: Let the noise of the day settle, then ask yourself the surah's question: about what am I asking?
Underneath the small questions, what to eat, what to say, what to reply, there may be a bigger one, maybe about death, or meaning, or whether you're loved, or what comes after.
Don't answer it; just find it, name it quietly in a few words, and let it sit, the way the surah lets its question sit.

wordCard.voice: An-Naba'. The news, news of great weight: the name of Surah 78, the first surah of the thirtieth part, which opens with the question about what. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the great news (78:2). naba' is weightier than khabar, everyday news.

carryVoice: Your line: the great news. Not the weather: news that changes something. Day two hundred nineteen.
